final_headline: The New Siri Is Here. What It Can Do, and Which iPhones Get It
seo_title: New Siri AI Features: What They Do, Which iPhones Get Them
seo_description: Apple's Siri AI can now understand your messages and screen, and has its own app. Here's what changed, which devices qualify, and what to try first.
summary: Apple's long-promised smarter Siri arrived with its fall software updates. It understands more of your personal context, can see what's on your screen, and now has an app of its own. Here is what it does, and who gets it.

article_body.text: For years, Siri was the assistant people used to set timers and not much else. With the software updates Apple released on September 14, that changes. Apple calls the new version Siri AI, and it is the biggest overhaul of the assistant since it arrived on the iPhone.
It is still labeled a beta, and it isn't on every device. But if you have a recent iPhone, it is worth ten minutes of your time to see what it can now do.
What is actually new

Apple describes the new Siri as more capable and conversational, with an understanding of your personal context, broad knowledge of the world and awareness of what is on your screen. In plain terms, that means three things.

items: It can use your own information. Apple says Siri can draw on context across your messages, emails and photos to help you find things. For example, it could find the address a friend texted you last week.
It knows what you are looking at. You can ask about what is on the screen in front of you, or ask it to get up-to-date information from the web.
It can help you write. With a feature Apple calls Write with Siri, you describe what you need and it produces a draft, or helps refine something you have already written.

article_body.text: Apple has also built Siri into the Camera app with a new Siri mode, so you can point your phone at something and ask about it. We explain how to use that in a separate guide.
Siri now has its own app

The most visible change is a dedicated Siri app. It gives you a place to see your past conversations with Siri and pick up where you left off, instead of each request disappearing once it is answered.
Apple says the app uses iCloud to privately sync your conversation history across your Apple devices. That means you can start a conversation on your iPhone and continue it on your iPad or Mac.

article_body.title: A privacy note
article_body.text: Syncing conversation history is convenient, but it also means your history is kept. If you share an Apple device with family members, or prefer not to keep a record, check the Siri app's settings before you start using it for personal matters.
Which devices get it
Siri AI needs fairly recent hardware. According to Apple, it is available on:

items: iPhone 16 models and later, plus iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max
iPad models with an M1 chip or later, and the iPad mini with the A17 Pro chip
Macs with an M1 chip or later
Apple Watch Series 9 or later, Apple Watch Ultra 2 or later, and Apple Watch SE 3
Apple Vision Pro

article_body.text: If you have an iPhone 15 or iPhone 15 Plus (not the Pro), or an older model, you will not get Siri AI, even after updating. Your current Siri will keep working as before.
Language and location limits
At launch, Siri AI is available in English as a beta. Apple says French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish are coming in October. It is not available to users under 13.

There are regional limits too. Apple says that in the European Union it is initially available only on Mac and Apple Vision Pro, and it is not available in China while Apple works through regulatory requirements.
Five things to try first

items: Ask it to find something you know is in your messages: "What time did Karen say dinner was on Saturday?"
Open a web page or a long email and ask, "Summarize this for me."
Ask a follow-up without repeating yourself. The new Siri is designed to keep the thread of a conversation.
Draft a short note: "Help me write a thank-you message to my neighbor for watering the plants." Then edit it before sending.
Open the Siri app later in the day and look back at what you asked. That is the easiest way to get a feel for how the history works.

article_body.text: What to keep in mind

A beta label means Apple expects rough edges. Siri AI may misunderstand requests, or answer confidently and get details wrong, as any AI assistant can. Double-check anything that matters, such as a date, a dollar figure or medical information, before you act on it.

It is also worth remembering what personal context means in practice. For Siri to find that address or dinner time, it has to work with your messages and email. Apple's approach is built around privacy, but you should still decide deliberately how much you want to rely on it for sensitive matters.
Should you turn it on?
If you have a supported device and use Siri even occasionally, yes, it is worth trying. The jump from the old Siri is large, and the new app makes it easier to use for more than quick commands.
If your iPhone isn't supported, there is no reason to rush an upgrade on Siri's account alone. The assistant will keep improving, and more devices and languages are already on Apple's schedule.

key_takeaways: Apple released Siri AI, a much more capable Siri, as a beta with its September 14 software updates.
It can use personal context from messages, email and photos, understand what's on screen, and help you write.
A new Siri app keeps your conversation history, synced privately across devices through iCloud.
It needs an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 or later; iPhone 15 and 15 Plus are not supported.
English only at launch; more languages in October; not in China, and limited in the EU at first.

final_headline: ChatGPT's New 'Dots' Keep Working After You Close the App. Here's What That Means
seo_title: What Are ChatGPT Dots? OpenAI's Always-On Agents, Explained
seo_description: OpenAI's new dots are AI agents that keep working between conversations. Here's what they do, who can use them now, and why it matters even if you can't.
summary: At its developer conference on September 29, OpenAI introduced dots: AI agents inside ChatGPT that keep working on a task between your conversations. They are starting with a limited group of paying customers. The idea behind them is worth understanding now.

article_body.text: For most people, ChatGPT works like a conversation. You ask, it answers, and nothing happens until you ask again. On September 29, OpenAI announced something that works differently.

It calls them dots. They are AI agents that live inside ChatGPT and keep working on an assignment between your conversations, rather than waiting for your next message. OpenAI unveiled them at DevDay, its annual event in San Francisco.
Most ChatGPT users won't see dots right away. But they are a clear sign of where AI assistants are heading, and that direction affects everyone who uses them.
What a dot actually is
Think of the difference between asking a question and hiring help. A normal chat answers a question. A dot is closer to giving a standing assignment to an assistant who keeps at it.

According to OpenAI and reporting from outlets including TechCrunch and VentureBeat, dots are powered by GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI's most capable model, released earlier in September. OpenAI says each dot has its own computer and web browser to work with. It can keep working around the clock and learn from your feedback over time.
OpenAI also introduced Spaces, shared areas where dots and the people on a team can work on the same project.
Who can use them now

OpenAI is starting dots with a limited set of paid ChatGPT plans for individuals and businesses. Because rollouts like this change quickly, the most reliable way to check whether you have access is to look in your own ChatGPT account, or on OpenAI's announcement page.
That pattern is typical for OpenAI: new capabilities usually start with paying customers and reach other plans later, if at all.
Why this matters even if you can't use them

Dots belong to a broader shift across the industry. In September alone, Microsoft introduced Autopilot, a Copilot agent it describes as persistent and proactive, and Meta launched Muse, a personal agent that can shop and handle email on your behalf.
The common idea is AI that doesn't just answer but acts, and keeps acting when you look away. That raises practical questions for ordinary users, even before these tools reach their plans.

items: What is it allowed to do? An agent with a browser can fill in forms and visit sites. The boundaries you set matter more than they did with a chatbot.
How do you know what it did? A standing assistant needs a record of its actions that you can check.

What does it cost? OpenAI hasn't published consumer pricing for dots beyond the plans that include them. Always-on work uses more computing power than a quick chat, and that cost has to land somewhere.

article_body.title: A sensible rule for any AI agent
article_body.text: Give it the smallest job and the fewest permissions that get the work done, and keep your own approval on anything that sends, spends or deletes. That applies to dots, to Microsoft's Autopilot and to any agent that reaches your plan next.
A plain-English glossary
These announcements come wrapped in jargon. Four terms are worth knowing.

items: Agent: AI that takes actions toward a goal, such as visiting websites or filling in forms, rather than only answering questions.
Always-on: an agent that keeps working on its assignment between your messages, instead of stopping when a conversation ends.
Computer use: an agent operating a computer or browser itself, clicking and typing much as a person would.
Permissions: the accounts, files and actions you allow an agent to reach. They are the most important setting you control.

article_body.text: What an everyday user might do with one

OpenAI's early examples lean toward work. But it is easy to picture household uses once agents like these become more widely available: tracking prices on a big purchase, monitoring a delayed refund, or keeping a running summary of your town's council meetings.
Those are useful jobs. They also involve your accounts, your money or your time, which is exactly why the questions above matter.
What to do now
If you don't see dots in your ChatGPT account, nothing changes for you today. Your ChatGPT still works the way it did last week.

Nor is this a reason to upgrade. Dots are new, and early versions of any agent tend to be rough. If your current plan does what you need today, it is sensible to wait and see how dots work in practice, and whether they reach more affordable plans.

If you do have access, start with a low-stakes assignment that doesn't touch money or private accounts, and watch what the agent does before you trust it with more. Read what it reports back, not just its conclusions.

And whichever assistant you use, it's worth knowing what it can already see. If you have connected your email or calendar, review those connections. Our guide to AI assistants and your email explains how.

key_takeaways: OpenAI announced dots on September 29: AI agents in ChatGPT that keep working between conversations.
Dots run on GPT-6 Astra and, OpenAI says, have their own computer and browser.
They are starting with a limited set of paid plans; check your own ChatGPT account to see whether you have access.
Microsoft and Meta announced similar 'always-on' agents in September; this is an industry-wide shift.
For any agent, grant the fewest permissions possible and keep approval on anything that sends, spends or deletes.

final_headline: Soon, Some Ads Will Have to Tell You the 'Person' Is AI
seo_title: California's New Law: Ads Must Disclose AI-Generated Actors
seo_description: California's SB 1050 requires video and audio ads to disclose when a performer was made with AI. Here's what it covers, when it starts and what it means.
summary: Governor Newsom signed SB 1050 on September 16, making California the second state, after New York, to require ads to say when a performer was created with AI. Here is what the law covers and what it doesn't.

article_body.text: The friendly woman recommending a supplement. The man in the kitchen who can't believe how easy the new mop is. The reassuring voice explaining a Medicare plan. Increasingly, some of these people don't exist. They were generated by AI.

California has decided you have a right to know. On September 16, Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 1050, which requires advertisers to disclose when an ad features a performer created with generative AI.
The law is short, but it touches something most viewers now wonder about at least occasionally while watching a commercial: is that person real?
California is the second state to do so, after New York. Because so much American advertising is made in, or aimed at, California, the effect is likely to reach well beyond the state.
What the law requires

SB 1050 applies to video and audio advertisements that include what the law calls a synthetic performer. That is a digital figure, voice or representation created at least in part with generative AI, realistic enough to give the impression of a real human performance.
When such a performer is used, the ad must carry a clear and conspicuous disclosure. The law says the wording should be substantially similar to one of two phrases:

items: "This performance features a synthetic performer."
"No human performer is depicted."

article_body.text: According to legal analyses of the law, the requirement is aimed at performers who carry the ad. That covers a performer demonstrating the product, delivering the main sales message, or reacting to it in a way that works like a testimonial.
When it starts

The bill was signed on September 16, 2026. The Legislature's official record lists it as a non-urgency statute, and under California's constitution a non-urgency law passed in a regular session takes effect on January 1 of the following year. That makes the start date January 1, 2027, which matches what law firms advising advertisers, including DLA Piper, have said. So you may not see the labels right away.
What it does not cover

The law has deliberate limits. It does not apply to ads for expressive works such as films, television shows, streaming series, documentaries and video games, provided the AI use in the ad matches its use in the work itself. It also carves out certain uses, such as language translation and accessibility features.
It is also not a general AI-labeling law. It doesn't require labels on social media posts, AI-written text or images in print ads. And it only governs advertising, not the scams that imitate it.

article_body.title: The label won't catch scams
article_body.text: A disclosure law binds legitimate advertisers. Criminals running fake endorsement videos, such as a celebrity who never agreed to promote a product, won't add a label. If an ad pushes you to pay quickly, buy through an unfamiliar link or trust a famous face, check it independently. Our guide to spotting AI-made photos and video explains how.
Why a normal person should care
Testimonials work because we trust people who seem like us. A realistic AI performer can deliver the reassuring expression and the "it changed my life" line without any real experience behind it.

A required label restores a little of the information you used to be able to assume: that the person in the ad was at least a real person. It also sets a norm other states may copy. The actors' union SAG-AFTRA backed the bill, and New York passed a similar law first.
The law covers audio ads as well as video. That matters for radio and podcast advertising, where a warm, trustworthy voice does much of the selling and there's no face to judge at all.
How to use this in practice

items: Starting next year, look for the disclosure line in California-facing video and audio ads, usually on screen or read aloud.
Treat a synthetic testimonial the way you would a paid actor: as a performance, not evidence that the product works.
For health products, financial services and anything aimed at older adults, look past the spokesperson to the terms, the fine print and independent reviews.
If an ad seems designed to rush you, slow down. That rule predates AI, and it still works.

article_body.text: If an ad looks deceptive

You don't need to wait for next year's labels to act on an ad that seems dishonest. The Federal Trade Commission collects reports of deceptive advertising and scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, and those reports help it spot patterns and bring cases.

If the ad appeared on a social platform, use the platform's own report option as well. That is often the fastest way to get a fake endorsement taken down. And if you lost money, contact your bank or card issuer right away.
The bottom line

SB 1050 won't stop AI from appearing in advertising, and it isn't meant to. It asks for honesty about who, or what, is doing the selling. For viewers, that is a small but real improvement, and a useful reminder to judge the product, not the face selling it.

key_takeaways: California's SB 1050, signed September 16, 2026, requires ads to disclose AI-generated 'synthetic performers.'
The disclosure must read substantially like 'This performance features a synthetic performer' or 'No human performer is depicted.'
Legal analyses say the requirements take effect January 1, 2027.
Ads for films, TV and video games are exempt when the AI use matches the work itself.
Scammers won't label their fakes, so the law is no substitute for checking suspicious ads yourself.

final_headline: The 'Officer' on the Video Call May Be Fake. What the FBI Wants You to Know
seo_title: FBI Warns of Fake Police and Officials on AI Video Calls
seo_description: The FBI says scammers posing as police and government officials now use AI to appear on video calls. Here's how the scam works and how to shut it down.
summary: On September 17, the FBI warned that criminals posing as police, court officers and government officials have cost Americans $1.6 billion since January 2025, and that some now use AI to appear on video calls. Here's how the scheme works and the one habit that defeats it.

article_body.text: The call comes on an ordinary afternoon. A man identifies himself as a sheriff's deputy. You missed jury duty, he says, and there is a warrant for your arrest. It can be resolved today, but only if you pay a fine right now, and you mustn't tell anyone, because that would complicate the case.
If you push back, he offers to prove it. A video call opens, and there he is: a uniform, a badge, an office behind him.
On September 17, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center issued a public warning about exactly this kind of fraud. It is not new. What is new is how convincing it has become.
How big the problem is
According to the FBI, between January 2025 and July 2026 it received nearly 61,000 complaints about scammers impersonating law enforcement or government officials, with losses of about $1.6 billion.
The FBI broke out several common versions:

items: Missed jury duty or a missed court date: 6,833 complaints and about $36 million in losses.
Problems with a professional license: 3,322 complaints and about $37 million lost.
Claims involving foreign governments or extradition: 1,809 complaints and about $140 million lost.
Expired or suspended licenses: 496 complaints and about $348,000 lost.

article_body.text: Where AI comes in

The FBI's warning is direct: scammers are using new technologies, including artificial intelligence, to support these impersonation schemes, and those technologies let them appear as law enforcement and government officials on video calls.

That removes one of the old safeguards. Many people have learned to be suspicious of a voice on the phone. A face on a screen, in uniform, is far more persuasive. It may be an AI-generated face or a real scammer made to look official.
Scammers also spoof real phone numbers, email addresses, employee names and credentials, the FBI says. So the caller ID may really show your county sheriff's number.
The pattern to recognize

The details change, but the FBI describes a consistent script. The caller is urgent and often aggressive. You are told to keep the call secret, sometimes even from family. You are accused of something, such as a missed court date or a license problem, and offered a way to make it go away. And you are told to pay in an unusual way.

That last point gives the game away. The FBI lists the payment methods these scammers demand: prepaid cards, cryptocurrency, bank wires, and cash deposited into cryptocurrency kiosks. No legitimate court or police department collects fines this way over the phone.

article_body.title: The one habit that defeats this scam
article_body.text: Hang up and call back using a number you look up yourself, from the official website of the court, sheriff's office or agency, or from a letter you already have. Never use a number, link or video link the caller gives you. A real officer will not object; a scammer will.
What to do if you get one of these calls

items: Don't pay, and don't share personal details such as your Social Security number, bank information or date of birth.
End the call, even if the caller threatens you. Real warrants are not resolved by phone payment.
Look up the agency's official number yourself and call to ask whether there is any issue.
Tell someone you trust. Scammers insist on secrecy precisely because a second opinion ends the scam.
Report it to your local police and to the FBI at ic3.gov, with any numbers, messages or payment details you have.

article_body.text: Texts and emails get the same treatment

Not every version starts with a call. The FBI says these scammers also use texts and emails, and spoof real email addresses and employee names. Its advice is to inspect web addresses carefully, because a fake site can differ from the real one by a single letter or an extra word.

The safest approach is not to use links in unexpected messages at all. If a message says you owe a fine or have a legal problem, type the agency's address into your browser yourself, or call the number printed on an official letter you already have.
If you already paid

Move quickly. Contact your bank or the payment service immediately to try to stop or reverse the transfer, and report the crime to local police and ic3.gov. Keep every record: call logs, texts, receipts from a crypto kiosk. Be wary of anyone who contacts you afterward offering to recover your money for a fee. That is a common second scam.
Talk about it before it happens

These scams work because they create panic and isolation in the moment. The best protection is a conversation you have ahead of time. Tell parents, grandparents and friends about this pattern, and agree that anyone who gets such a call will hang up and phone a family member first.
It is the same principle as a family code word against voice-cloning calls. When a stranger demands secrecy and immediate payment, the safest move is to break the secrecy.

key_takeaways: The FBI warned on September 17 about scammers impersonating police and government officials.
It counts nearly 61,000 complaints and about $1.6 billion in losses from January 2025 to July 2026.
The FBI says scammers now use AI to appear as officials on video calls, and spoof real phone numbers.
Demands for payment by prepaid card, crypto, wire or crypto kiosk are a giveaway; courts don't collect fines that way.
Hang up and call the agency back on a number you look up yourself; report to ic3.gov.

final_headline: Your Android Phone Can Now Remember Where You Put Your Passport
seo_title: How to Make Gemini Remember Where You Put Things on Android
seo_description: A new Android feature lets Gemini remember where you left important items, and another reads fine print aloud. Here's how both work and who gets them.
summary: Google's September Android update added two small AI features with real everyday value: Gemini can now remember where you put things, and a new Guided Vision mode can read small print aloud. Here's how to use them.

article_body.text: Everyone has a drawer or shelf where the important things go: the passport, the spare car key, the warranty for the dishwasher. And everyone has had the afternoon when they couldn't remember which drawer.

Google's September update for Android phones includes a simple fix. You can tell Gemini, Google's AI assistant, where you put something, and it will remember for you. A second new feature uses your phone's camera to read fine print aloud.
Neither will change your life. Both are the kind of small, practical AI that is easy to underrate, and both come with the update at no extra cost.
Tell Gemini where you put it

Google's Find Hub app, formerly Find My Device, has always helped locate phones, earbuds and items with Bluetooth tracker tags. Now it can also keep track of things that have no tracker at all, because you tell it.
Google's example: "Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in my bedroom drawer." You can add a photo, too, which helps when "the drawer" could mean several.
Later, ask Gemini where your passport is, or open the new Remembered items tab in Find Hub to see everything you have saved.
Good things to remember this way

items: Passports, birth certificates and other documents you rarely touch.
Spare keys, including the one you gave a neighbor.
Seasonal items: holiday decorations, the snow shovel, the patio umbrella.
Where you parked in a large garage, with a photo of the level sign.
The location of the water shut-off valve or the circuit breaker, for whoever might need it.

article_body.title: Keep it practical, not sensitive
article_body.text: It's a convenience, not a vault. Saying where you keep valuables creates a record in your Google account. For cash, jewelry or anything you would not want someone else to find, a written note kept somewhere safe may be the wiser choice.
Who gets it

Google says the remembered-items feature requires Android 16 or later, in countries where both Gemini and Find Hub are available. If your phone runs an older version of Android, it won't appear, even after the update.
To check your version, open Settings, then About phone, and look for the Android version.
Guided Vision: help reading the small print
The second feature is aimed at accessibility, but many people will find it useful. Guided Vision is a mode of Gemini Live that uses your phone's camera to describe what it sees in real time.

Google gives three examples: reading the fine print on a food label, ordering from a menu in a dimly lit restaurant, and identifying household objects. Unlike simply taking a photo and zooming in, Guided Vision talks you through it. It tells you how to move the phone to frame the text properly, then reads it back.
For anyone whose eyesight isn't what it was, that could mean fewer moments squinting at a pill bottle or asking a server to read the specials.
How to turn on Guided Vision

Google says you can start Guided Vision in three ways: add it to your phone's accessibility shortcuts, open it from the TalkBack menu if you use the TalkBack screen reader, or turn it on in the Gemini app's settings.
Google describes it as coming soon to phones running Android 9 or later where Gemini is available. So if you don't see it yet, it may simply not have reached your phone.
A word of caution on reading labels

For food allergies and medications, use Guided Vision as a helper, not the final check. Camera-based reading can misread small or curved text. When the stakes are high, confirm with the pharmacist, the manufacturer or someone you trust.
Also in the same update
Google's September update included a few other changes worth knowing about.

items: Motion Assist: an optional screen overlay designed to reduce motion sickness when you use your phone in a moving car. Google says it requires Android 17.
Google Keep in Messages: you can now collaborate on a shared note, such as a grocery list, directly inside a Google Messages conversation.
Chat personalization: custom backgrounds and color themes for individual conversations in Google Messages, which makes it easier to tell family chats apart at a glance.

article_body.text: The bigger picture

These features point to a quieter side of AI. Not the chatbot that writes essays, but the phone that helps you find the passport before the flight and read the label in a dim store aisle. It is worth ten minutes to set up, especially the next time you put something important "somewhere safe."

A simple way to start: walk through the house once with your phone and tell Gemini where five important things live: your passport, the spare keys, the warranty folder, your medication list and any emergency cash. The next time one of them goes missing, you will be glad you did.

key_takeaways: Google's September Android update lets you tell Gemini where you put items; they appear in a Remembered tab in Find Hub.
You can attach a photo, and later just ask Gemini where the item is.
Remembered items need Android 16 or later, where Gemini and Find Hub are available.
Guided Vision in Gemini Live reads fine print and menus aloud, guiding you to frame the camera.

final_headline: Microsoft's New Copilot Wants to Do the Work, Not Just Help. What Office Workers Should Know
seo_title: Microsoft's New Copilot and Autopilot, Explained for Workers
seo_description: Microsoft's rebuilt Copilot adds Cowork, Office inside Copilot and an always-on agent called Autopilot. Here's what each does and when you might see it.
summary: On September 25, Microsoft introduced a rebuilt Copilot for work, including an agent called Autopilot that keeps working when you don't. Here's what each piece does, when employees might actually see it, and what to ask your employer.

article_body.text: If you use Word, Excel, Outlook or Teams at work, Microsoft has just announced the biggest change in years to how those tools will fit together, and AI is at the center of it.

On September 25, Microsoft introduced what it calls the new Copilot. It pulls chat, delegated tasks and the Office apps into one place, and adds an agent called Autopilot that keeps working on assignments while you do something else.
Most workers won't see all of this right away. But it is worth understanding now, because it will shape the next few years of office work for a lot of people.
The pieces, in plain English
Microsoft's announcement has several named parts. Here is what each one is, based on Microsoft's own descriptions.

items: Home: a new starting screen where you can review recent activity, get suggestions and pick up unfinished work. It is where chat and Cowork come together.

Cowork: a mode for handing off a whole task. You define the job, such as responding to a request for proposal or preparing a product launch kit, and Copilot runs it end to end and returns a finished result.
Office in Copilot: Word, Excel and PowerPoint built into Copilot itself. You can ask it to draft a brief, model a budget or build a slide deck, and get real, editable documents.
Code: a way for people who aren't programmers to describe an app, tracker, dashboard or automation in plain language and have Copilot build it.
Autopilot: what Microsoft calls a persistent, proactive and personal agent that keeps working even when you're not. You give it a name, a role and a goal.

article_body.text: When you might actually see it

Microsoft is rolling this out in stages. Home and Code start with the Frontier program, Microsoft's early-access program for business customers, in the coming weeks. Autopilot is expanding to a private preview at the end of the month. Microsoft says a preview of Code for Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers will follow later in 2026.
In practice, most employees will see these features when their company's IT department turns them on, not before. Some organizations will move quickly; many will wait.
A change in how Copilot is paid for

Microsoft is also changing its pricing approach. Everyday Copilot use in chat and the Office apps is covered by a fixed per-user subscription. More advanced capabilities, including Cowork, Code and Autopilot, run on usage-based billing, so the cost depends on how much work the AI does.
For employees, that matters indirectly. Usage-based features tend to come with limits and approvals, so don't be surprised if your company restricts who can use Autopilot, and for what.

article_body.title: Before you delegate real work
article_body.text: An AI that produces a finished deliverable can also produce a finished mistake. Treat Cowork output like work from a new colleague: check the numbers, the claims and anything sent in your name before it leaves your hands.
What an always-on agent means for your job

Autopilot is the part that has drawn the most attention, and it fits a wider trend. OpenAI launched always-on agents called dots in ChatGPT on September 29. The idea is the same: AI that keeps working between your instructions.

For workers, the realistic near-term effect is less about replacement and more about supervision. Someone still sets the goal, checks the work and takes responsibility for it. People who are good at explaining a task clearly and judging the result will get more out of these tools than those who aren't.
Five questions to ask your employer

items: Is the new Copilot, or Autopilot, approved for our team, and for what kinds of work?
What company data can it reach, such as email, files and customer records, and who decides?
Who is accountable when an AI-produced document has an error?
Is there training, and time to learn it properly?
How will its use be measured, if at all?

article_body.text: If you use Microsoft 365 at home or for a small business

Most of this announcement is aimed at companies. But Microsoft says a preview of Code will come to Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later in 2026. If you pay for Microsoft 365 yourself, as a freelancer or a small business owner, you may be able to try it before many employees can.

Code is designed for people who don't write software. You describe a tool, such as an invoice tracker or a simple sign-up form, in plain language, and Copilot builds it. Microsoft says it runs in a protected environment. As with anything that handles customer or financial data, test it with made-up information first.
What to do this week

You don't need to do anything yet. But if your company already offers Copilot, it is a good time to get comfortable with the basics, such as drafting in Word or summarizing an email thread, so the bigger features feel familiar when they arrive.
And keep your own judgment in the loop. Microsoft's pitch is AI that does more of the work. The workers who do best will be the ones who stay clear about which parts of the work are still theirs.

key_takeaways: Microsoft announced a rebuilt Copilot on September 25 with Home, Cowork, Office in Copilot, Code and Autopilot.
Autopilot is a persistent agent that keeps working when you're not; it's in private preview.
Home and Code start with Microsoft's Frontier early-access program; most workers will see features only when IT enables them.
Advanced features like Cowork, Code and Autopilot move to usage-based billing, likely with limits.
Check AI-produced work before it goes out in your name, and ask your employer what the tools can access.

final_headline: Gemini Notebook Can Now Record Your Thoughts and Talk Back. Here's How to Use It Well
seo_title: Gemini Notebook's New Recorder and Voice Chat, Explained
seo_description: Google's Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) adds an audio recorder and live voice conversations with your notes. Here's how they work at work and at home.
summary: Google's Gemini Notebook, the tool once called NotebookLM, now lets you record audio on your phone and hold a spoken conversation with your notebook. Here's how to use both features well, and where to be careful.

article_body.text: Some of the best ideas arrive at the worst times: in the car, on a walk, halfway through a meeting when you can't type. Google's Gemini Notebook, the research tool many people still know as NotebookLM, now has two features built for exactly those moments.

Google announced them on September 18, with a rollout that began September 15. The mobile app can now record audio, and you can hold a spoken, back-and-forth conversation with the material in a notebook.
What Gemini Notebook is, briefly

Gemini Notebook works differently from a general chatbot. You create a notebook and add sources, such as documents, web pages and notes, and it answers questions based on those sources rather than on the whole internet. That makes it well suited to work projects, research and anything where you need answers you can trace back to the original.
The new features build on that idea. Instead of typing questions into a notebook at your desk, you can now feed it your spoken thoughts and question it out loud.
New: an audio recorder in the mobile app

The Gemini Notebook app for Android and iPhone now includes an audio recorder. Google frames it for students capturing lectures, but it is just as useful for recording your own thoughts on the go. Google says the recordings sit directly alongside the sources in your notebook, so they can be cited and edited like the rest of your material.
Practical uses at work include:

items: Talking through a plan on your commute, then asking the notebook to turn it into an outline.
Recording your own notes right after a meeting, while the details are fresh.
Capturing a training session or presentation you are allowed to record, to review later.

article_body.text: A simple first test: record two minutes of thoughts about a project, then ask the notebook to turn them into an outline and to list any open questions you mentioned. You'll quickly see whether talking suits you better than typing.

article_body.title: Ask before you record other people
article_body.text: Recording a meeting or conversation can be subject to your employer's policies and, in some states, laws requiring everyone's consent. When others are speaking, get permission first. The safest default is to record yourself, not the room.
New: talk to your notebook

The second feature turns a notebook into something you can speak with. Using the mobile app, you can have a real-time conversation with a notebook: ask questions aloud, get step-by-step explanations, and interrupt with follow-ups, as you would with a person.
Google says every answer is grounded in your sources, which is the key difference from a general voice assistant. It works in nearly 100 languages. The feature is limited to users 18 and older.

For work, that makes it a useful way to prepare. Load the documents for tomorrow's meeting, then ask questions out loud while you make coffee: "What are the three open issues in this contract?" or "Quiz me on the new policy."
Who can use these features

Google says these updates are available to all Google Workspace customers and Workspace Individual subscribers, and to people with personal Google accounts. Because the rollout is gradual, it may take a couple of weeks or more to appear in your app.
If you use a work account, your company's administrator may control which Google features are turned on, so check with IT if you don't see them.
Other new learning tools
The same update added features Google aimed at students. They are just as handy for workplace training or getting up to speed on a new subject.

items: Interactive learning overviews that combine a summary with quizzes, flashcards and mind maps.
More quiz formats, including short answer, multiple choice and fill-in-the-blank, for testing yourself on the material.
Short Video Overviews of about a minute, available in more than 80 languages, that explain a notebook's material.

article_body.text: For a new policy, a certification or a product you have to learn quickly, a self-quiz built from the actual documents is a useful way to check what has sunk in.
Using it well

items: Keep each notebook focused on one project, so answers draw only on relevant sources.
Name recordings clearly, such as "Q4 budget thoughts, Oct 2," so they are easy to find later.
When the notebook gives you an important answer, open the cited source to confirm it.
Don't upload or record confidential material unless your employer has approved the tool for it.

article_body.text: The limits

Grounded answers are more trustworthy than a general chatbot's, but not infallible. The tool can still misread a passage or leave out a qualification. It only knows what you put in, too, so an answer is only as current as your sources.

Used with those limits in mind, the recorder and the voice conversation make Gemini Notebook more useful for busy people who think better out loud than at a keyboard. For a comparison with other document tools, see our guide to summarizing long documents.

key_takeaways: Google's Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) added an audio recorder to its Android and iOS apps; rollout began Sept. 15.
Recordings sit alongside your sources so they can be cited and edited.
You can now hold a real-time spoken conversation with a notebook, grounded in its sources, in nearly 100 languages (18+ only).
Available to Workspace customers, Workspace Individual subscribers and personal Google accounts, as the rollout reaches them.
Get permission before recording others, and verify important answers against the cited source.

final_headline: Meta's New AI Glasses, Compared: Which Pair (If Any) Makes Sense for You
seo_title: Meta AI Glasses 2026: Audio vs. Gen 3 vs. Adventurer
seo_description: Meta's lineup now includes the audio-only Ray-Ban Meta Audio, from $349, alongside camera models. We compare prices, features and privacy.
summary: At its Connect event on September 23, Meta widened its lineup of AI glasses, including an audio-only pair with no camera. Here's how the options compare on price, features and privacy, and who each one suits.

article_body.text: Smart glasses have gone from a curiosity to something you can buy in a regular eyewear shop. At its annual Connect event on September 23, Meta widened the choice again. The most interesting addition for many people is a pair with no camera at all.
If you have been curious about hands-free music, calls or an AI assistant in your glasses, here is how the main options now compare, and how to decide whether any of them is worth it.
The lineup at a glance

items: Ray-Ban Meta Audio, from $349: audio-only, with no camera. Music, podcasts, calls and a hands-free AI assistant. Preorders opened September 23, and Meta says it ships October 13.

Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3), from $449, available now: a 12-megapixel camera with 3K Ultra HD video and up to nine hours of battery life. Styles include Wayfarer, Aviator and a new cat-eye frame called Zena.
Meta Adventurer, from $249: a low-cost model in Meta's own Meta Glasses line.

article_body.text: Prices and dates are from Meta's own announcement. Check current prices with the retailer, since frames, lenses and prescriptions change the total.
Why a camera-free pair is a big deal

The camera has always been the most controversial part of smart glasses. People around you can't always tell whether you are recording, and some places, such as gyms, doctors' offices and many workplaces, don't welcome it.

Ray-Ban Meta Audio removes that question entirely. Meta describes it as having the power of earbuds and AI, and lists no camera among its features; launch coverage from Bloomberg, Engadget and TechCrunch confirms it has none. Meta says the glasses weigh 43 grams and run up to 12 hours on a charge, with up to 48 more hours from the included case. They come in two styles, Clubmaster and Burbank, with 23 color and lens combinations, and both work with a wide range of prescriptions.
For many people over 50, that may be the most practical version yet: good audio, hands-free calls and an assistant, without the social awkwardness of a camera on your face.
When the camera models make sense

The camera versions are built for people who want to capture what they see. That could be grandchildren at the park without holding up a phone, a hike, or a recipe they want to remember. The camera also lets the AI assistant see what you are looking at and answer questions about it.
Meta says the Gen 3 camera takes 12-megapixel photos and 3K Ultra HD video. A built-in LED light, Meta says, helps make people around you aware when you're taking photos or video.

article_body.title: Mind the etiquette, and the rules
article_body.text: If you choose a camera pair, ask before recording people, take them off in private settings, and check the rules at work and in medical offices. A small recording light is easy for others to miss.
What about the AI assistant?

Meta says its glasses now connect to Muse, its new personal AI agent, so you can use it without reaching for your phone. That makes it a good moment to think about what you want an assistant to do from your glasses, and what you'd rather keep on your phone, where you can see it.
How to choose

items: Decide on the camera first. If you mainly want audio, calls and the assistant, the Audio pair is simpler and avoids privacy friction.
Try them on in person. Weight, fit over your ears and how the speakers sound in a noisy room matter more than specifications.
Check prescription options and the total cost with lenses, which can add substantially to the base price.
Consider battery life for how you'd actually use them. A day of calls is different from an hour of music.
Read the privacy settings in the Meta app before you connect your accounts.

article_body.text: Questions to ask before you pay

items: What is the return window, and does it still apply if prescription lenses have been fitted?
Can my prescription be fitted to this frame, and what will that add to the price?
What does the warranty cover, and who handles repairs?
Which phone and app do the glasses need, and does my phone qualify?
How loud do the speakers sound in a busy place, like a restaurant or a street?

article_body.text: A good store will let you listen to the speakers and try the voice assistant before you buy. If one won't, consider buying where it will.
Our take

For most readers who are curious but not sure, the camera-free Ray-Ban Meta Audio is the most sensible place to start. It does the everyday things well and avoids the biggest downside of smart glasses. Choose a camera model only if capturing photos and video hands-free is the main reason you want them.

key_takeaways: Meta announced audio-only Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses (from $349; ships Oct. 13) at Connect on Sept. 23.
Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 starts at $449 with a 12MP camera and 3K video; Meta Adventurer starts at $249.
Removing the camera eliminates most of the privacy and etiquette concerns around smart glasses.
Try glasses on in person and price in prescription lenses before buying.
Our pick for most curious buyers: start with the camera-free Audio pair.

final_headline: A Scam That Doesn't Need Your Password: How to See What Apps Can Get Into Your Accounts
seo_title: How to Check Which Apps Have Access to Your Accounts
seo_description: The FBI warns of consent phishing, which gets into accounts without a password. How it works, and how to review app access on Google, Microsoft and Apple.
summary: On September 1, the FBI warned about consent phishing: tricking people into approving a malicious app, which then gets into their account without ever needing the password. Here's how it works and a ten-minute checkup for your Google, Microsoft and Apple accounts.

article_body.text: Most of us have learned the rules for passwords: use strong ones, never share them, turn on two-step verification. Consent phishing is dangerous because it works around all of that.

On September 1, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center warned about this technique. It doesn't steal your password. It persuades you to approve an app, and the app then gets into your account on its own.
How consent phishing works

You have probably seen a legitimate version of this many times. You use a new service, and a screen asks: "Allow this app to access your Google account?" or "This app would like to read your email." You approve it, and the app can do what it asked, without ever learning your password.

That system is called OAuth, and it is how countless genuine apps connect to your accounts, including AI assistants that read your email or calendar. The FBI's warning is that criminals now build malicious apps to exploit the same approval screen.
According to the FBI, the scheme typically goes like this:

items: Criminals create an app and set it up to request broad permissions.

They message you, often pretending to be someone you know or trust. The FBI mentions impersonation of government officials and media personalities, and fake file-sharing or identity-verification services.
The message contains a link. You click, sign in normally on the real login page, and are shown a permission request.
If you approve it, the app can act on your behalf, reading your email and accessing your files.

article_body.text: Why it is so hard to stop

The FBI points out what makes consent phishing especially dangerous. Because you approved the app yourself, it bypasses both your password and your two-step verification. And changing your password afterward doesn't remove the app's access. It keeps working until you revoke it.
The FBI says these attacks have targeted prominent people, their family members and acquaintances, often through direct messages on messaging apps. But the technique works on anyone.

article_body.title: Read the permission screen
article_body.text: Before approving any app, read what it's asking for. A document-signing or 'verification' tool has no business reading all your email. If you didn't go looking for the app, don't approve it.
Red flags on a permission screen

items: You arrived from a link in an unexpected message, rather than by going to the app yourself.
The app's name is generic, misspelled or doesn't match the company that supposedly sent it.
It asks for far more than its job needs, such as reading, sending or deleting all your email.
The message behind it created urgency: a document that expires, an account to verify today, an official request.
You can't find the app on a reputable app store or the company's own website.

article_body.text: Your ten-minute account checkup
The good news is that every major account lets you see which apps have access and remove them. Do this once now, and again every few months.
Google account

Go to your Google Account, open Security, and find the section for third-party apps and services, where Google lists every app and service with access to your account data. Select any app you don't recognize or no longer use, and remove its access.
Microsoft account

For a personal Microsoft account, the kind you use for Outlook.com, Hotmail or Xbox, sign in at account.microsoft.com and look through the privacy and security settings for the list of apps and services you've allowed to access your account. Remove any you don't recognize or no longer use. Microsoft reorganizes these menus from time to time, so if you can't find the list, search Microsoft's support site for app permissions on your Microsoft account.
Work and school accounts are different: they are managed through your organization's My Apps portal, and your IT department may control what you can change.
Apple account

On an iPhone, open Settings, tap your name, then tap Sign in with Apple to see apps that use your Apple Account. Select one and tap Delete to stop using Sign in with Apple with it. Apple notes that if a developer uses one account across several apps, removing one removes them all.
What to remove

items: Anything you don't recognize.
Apps you tried once and forgot, such as quizzes, old photo editors and expired trials.
Services that ask for more than they need. A calendar app that can read all your email deserves a second look.
AI tools you no longer use. If you connected an assistant to your inbox and stopped using it, disconnect it.

article_body.text: If you think you approved a bad app

Remove its access immediately using the steps above; that is the step that actually cuts it off. Then change your password anyway, check your email's forwarding rules and recent account activity, and tell people in your contacts if messages may have been sent from your account. The FBI asks victims to report incidents to their local FBI field office or at ic3.gov.
The habit worth keeping

Treat "Allow access" the way you treat a request for your password. It isn't the same thing, but it can hand over nearly as much. When in doubt, don't approve. And put a reminder in your calendar to repeat this checkup a few times a year.

key_takeaways: The FBI warned on September 1 about consent phishing: tricking you into approving a malicious app.
Approved apps can read email and files without your password, bypassing two-step verification.
Changing your password doesn't remove an app's access; you must revoke it.
Review app access in your Google Account (Security), in your Microsoft account's privacy and security settings, and in Settings > Sign in with Apple.
Read every permission screen, and never approve an app you didn't go looking for.

final_headline: Point, Tap, Ask: How to Use Siri Mode in Your iPhone's Camera
seo_title: How to Use Siri Mode in the iPhone Camera (Step by Step)
seo_description: Siri mode in the iPhone Camera can identify objects, answer questions about what you see and take action. Here's how to use it, with practical examples.
summary: With Apple's new Siri AI, your iPhone camera can answer questions about whatever it's pointed at. Here's how to turn on Siri mode, what the buttons do, and the everyday uses that make it worth learning.

article_body.text: You're in a garden center looking at a plant with no label. You're at a friend's house admiring a lamp. You've found an odd little part in the junk drawer and have no idea what it belongs to. For moments like these, the iPhone camera now has a new trick.
It's called Siri mode, and it arrived with Apple's Siri AI update in September. Point your camera at something, tap, and ask. Here's how to use it.
What you need

According to Apple, Siri mode requires Siri AI, which is available in beta on iOS 27 or later. You also need an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or an iPhone 16 model or later. Siri and your device language must be set to a supported language; at launch, that's English.
If you have an older iPhone, or an iPhone 15 or 15 Plus, you won't see Siri mode. Our overview of the new Siri explains which devices qualify.
If you don't see Siri mode

First, check that your iPhone is updated to the latest version of iOS in Settings, under General and Software Update. Then make sure Siri AI (Beta) is turned on. Apple's guide describes Siri mode as something you can use once Siri AI is on.
Finally, check that both Siri and your iPhone's language are set to a supported language. At launch that means English, with more languages due in October.
Step 1: Open Siri mode
On iPhones with a Camera Control, the button on the side, press and hold it. Apple also offers other ways to open it on models without that button. Then tap Siri to switch the camera into Siri mode.
Point your iPhone at whatever you want to know about. Hold it steady and fill the frame with the object if you can.
Step 2: Choose what you want
Apple's support guide describes four things you can do once Siri mode is open.

items: Tap the Siri button for quick information about what's in the frame. Apple's example is pointing at an unfamiliar object and having Siri identify it.
Tap Ask to ask a specific question. Apple's example: point at a bunch of ingredients and ask, "What can I make with these?"
Tap Search to look for similar images on the web, handy for finding where to buy something you've seen.
Tap an action if one appears. Apple's example is pointing at a restaurant check and choosing to split the bill with Apple Cash.

article_body.text: Everyday uses worth trying

items: In the garden: "What plant is this, and does it need full sun?"
In the kitchen: point at what's in the fridge and ask for a simple dinner idea.
At the hardware store: photograph a worn part and search for a matching replacement.
Traveling: point at a sign or menu in another language and ask what it says.
Around the house: "What is this cable for?" when you find one in a drawer.

article_body.title: Treat answers as a good guess
article_body.text: Siri mode is part of a beta, and identifying things from a photo is hard. Plant names, product models and especially anything you might eat, take or plug in deserve a second check before you rely on the answer.
Tips for better results

items: Use good light. A dim kitchen or a shaded corner makes identification harder.
Fill the frame with one object at a time rather than a cluttered scene.
Get close to labels and text, and hold the phone steady for a moment.
Ask a follow-up. If Siri names a plant, ask how often to water it; if it names a part, ask what it fits.
If the first answer seems off, try a different angle before trusting it.

article_body.text: Where to be careful
Be thoughtful about pointing the camera at people. Asking an AI about a stranger raises obvious privacy questions, and it's not a use Apple highlights.

Be careful with documents, too. Pointing Siri mode at a bill or a letter can be helpful, but those often carry account numbers and personal details. Our guide to what not to tell an AI assistant covers the basics.
And for health questions, such as a rash, a pill or a symptom, use what you learn as a starting point for a conversation with a pharmacist or doctor, not a diagnosis.
Not on an iPhone?

Android phones have a similar idea. Google's Gemini Live can see through your camera, and its new Guided Vision mode reads fine print and menus aloud. We cover that in our story on Android's latest features.
Make it a habit

Like most new features, Siri mode is easy to forget. The trick is to try it the next three times you'd otherwise type a description into a search box: the plant, the part, the label. After that, reaching for it becomes natural.

key_takeaways: Siri mode in the Camera app lets you point at something and get information, ask questions, search or take action.
It needs Siri AI (beta, iOS 27+) on an iPhone 15 Pro/Pro Max or iPhone 16 or later, in a supported language.
On iPhones with Camera Control, press and hold it, then tap Siri.
Use Ask for specific questions and Search to find similar items online.
Treat identifications as a good guess, and avoid pointing it at people or sensitive documents.
